tagline: Flat farmland, Limbu and Lepcha villages and a tower of clay pots
meta_description: Daramdin, Soreng district: the Lepcha clay-pot tower story, Stairway to Heaven site, Limbu village homestays, farm walks, how to get there and costs.
summary: Daramdin is a market village at about 950 m in Soreng district, roughly 29 km above Jorethang on the road to Sombaria and Okhrey. Its name comes from the Lepcha word for flat land. Come for the clay-pot tower story and its Stairway to Heaven site, Limbu and Lepcha village homestays and quiet farm walks.
intro: Daramdin lies in the lower, warmer part of Soreng district, at about 950 m, on the road that climbs from Jorethang through Tharpu to Sombaria, Okhrey and Hilley. The district administration explains the name as coming from the Lepcha word dalom, a place of rest or flat land, and that fits: unusually for this steep country, Daramdin has broad, gently sloping fields of paddy, maize and vegetables around a small bazaar. It is also the seat of one of the district's six blocks.

Wikipedia notes that the area is home mostly to Limbu and Lepcha families, with Pradhan, Chettri, Bhujel and other Nepali-speaking households too. That mix is the reason to stay. Homestays here are simple family houses, and an evening with a Limbu or Lepcha host, eating home food and hearing family history, is closer to the real western Sikkim than any viewpoint. Daramdin has very few visitors, even in the busy months.

Daramdin's best-known story belongs to the Lepcha tradition: villagers who set out to measure the distance to the sky by building a tower of clay pots. The district site tells it in full, and the place linked to it, Swarga Janae Seeri or the Stairway to Heaven, has been under construction since its foundation in 1997. Add the Sri Sathya Sai Sarva Dharma Kendra in the village centre and a farm walk, and one night fills easily.

story.title: The Lepcha tower of clay pots
story.text: The Soreng district administration records a story attached to Daramdin from Lepcha tradition. Many centuries ago, it says, the villagers argued about how far their village was from the sky, and decided to find out by building a tower of clay pots, one on top of another. The tower rose higher and higher. When it was nearly at the sky, the man at the top shouted down in Lepcha, "Kok bing yang tal", asking for a pole to strike the sky. The men at the bottom heard only "cheka", which they took to mean destroy the ladder, and asked him to repeat it. They heard the same word again, pulled the tower down, and it fell. The district site adds that pieces of clay pots were found in Daramdin in later years. A memorial on the theme, Swarga Janae Seeri or Stairway to Heaven, had its foundation laid in 1997, according to Wikipedia. We tell the tale as the district does: a village tradition about ambition and misunderstanding, not a dated event.
story.source: Soreng district administration, soreng.nic.in (Daramdin; Stair Way to Heaven); Wikipedia: Daramdin

little_known.fact: The district administration explains Daramdin as coming from the Lepcha word dalom, meaning a place of rest or a flat land, a fitting name for one of the few broad, level farming areas in Soreng district.
Wikipedia records that the foundation of Swarga Janae Seeri, the Stairway to Heaven memorial tied to the clay-pot tower story, was laid in 1997; work stopped for years and later resumed.
Daramdin is one of the six administrative blocks of Soreng district, alongside Baiguney, Kaluk, Mangalbarey, Chumbong and Soreng, each run from its own block administrative centre.

highlights.title: Swarga Janae Seeri, the Stairway to Heaven
highlights.text: A memorial site tied to the Lepcha story of a tower of clay pots built to reach the sky. Wikipedia dates its foundation to 1997, and work has stopped and restarted since, so check current status before you travel. Even unfinished, it is the place to hear the story from local people.

highlights.title: Limbu and Lepcha village homestays
highlights.text: Daramdin's villages are mostly Limbu and Lepcha, with other Nepali-speaking families. Homestays here are simple family houses at about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals. Ask your hosts about their food, their festivals and their family histories; that is the real reason to stay.

highlights.title: Farm walks on the flat land
highlights.text: Daramdin's name means flat land, and its fields are easy walking by Sikkim standards. Paddy is transplanted around June and July and harvested in October and November, maize stands tall in summer, and oranges ripen around houses from November. The district site also lists rose farming here.

highlights.title: Sri Sathya Sai Sarva Dharma Kendra
highlights.text: Wikipedia names this centre in the middle of Daramdin as the village's main attraction. Sarva dharma means all faiths. It is a calm place to stop on the way through; dress modestly, remove shoes where asked and follow any timings posted at the gate.

highlights.title: Warm winters in the lower valley
highlights.text: At about 950 m, Daramdin is warmer than Rinchenpong or Okhrey: winter days often reach the high teens °C while the ridges stay cold. That makes it a comfortable stop for families and older travellers from November to February, and a good place to break the climb to Okhrey.

highlights.title: Gateway to Sombaria, Okhrey and Barsey
highlights.text: Daramdin sits on the road from Jorethang to Sombaria, about 7 km below Sombaria, with Okhrey and Hilley beyond. A night here lets you start the climb to the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary rested, and see a farming village that most Barsey visitors drive straight past.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Jorethang to Daramdin and Sombaria, about 1–1.5 hours to Daramdin for roughly ₹80–150 a seat. Morning departures are most frequent. From Siliguri, take a shared jeep to Jorethang (about 3.5–4 hours, ₹250–350) and change. Jeeps also link Daramdin with Soreng bazaar.

Daramdin is about 29 km from Jorethang via Nayabazar and Tharpu, about 15 km from Soreng and 7 km below Sombaria. Okhrey is roughly 20 km further up. A small car from Jorethang costs about ₹1,500–2,000 one way; from Gangtok, about 115–120 km and 5 hours, roughly ₹5,000–6,000.

The district gives about 120 km from Bagdogra to Daramdin, 4–5 hours by car via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang, about ₹4,500–6,000 for a small car. NH10 along the Teesta closes after monsoon slides, when drivers go via Kalimpong or Darjeeling. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Daramdin has family homestays rather than hotels. The district administration lists Dzoom Lyang Homestay, Sai Shruti Homestay and Orange Valley Homestay near the Stairway to Heaven site, and Red Chilli Village Resort in the area; confirm they are operating and what is included when you book. Expect ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals at homestays. For more choice, Soreng town is about 15 km away, and the Sherpa homestays of Okhrey are about 20 km up the road.
tips: Carry cash: Daramdin has small shops but you should draw money in Jorethang or Soreng.
Ask your homestay hosts before photographing family shrines, elders or rituals.
Visit in November or early December to see paddy harvest and oranges ripening at the same time.
Combine Daramdin with Tharpu's Mangardzong site, about 6 km down the road.
Check the current state of work at the Stairway to Heaven site locally before making a special trip.

experiences.title: The clay-pot tower story at Stairway to Heaven
experiences.summary: Visit Swarga Janae Seeri, the Stairway to Heaven site in Daramdin, and hear the Lepcha story of villagers who built a tower of clay pots to reach the sky. A short walk, told with a local guide, that explains how a village remembers itself.
body: The story comes from Lepcha tradition and is recorded by the Soreng district administration. Villagers in Daramdin argued about how far the sky was and began to build a tower of clay pots to find out. Near the top, the man at the summit called for a pole to strike the sky, "Kok bing yang tal" in Lepcha, but those below heard only "cheka", which they took to mean destroy the ladder. They brought the tower down. The district site says clay pot pieces were later found in Daramdin.

Swarga Janae Seeri, meaning stairway to heaven, is the memorial site built around that story. Wikipedia records that its foundation was laid in 1997, that construction stopped and that it later resumed. How finished it is when you visit will vary, so check current status before you travel. The point of coming is less the structure than hearing the story where it is told, ideally from someone whose family has told it for generations.

A local guide, about ₹500–800, can walk you there, tell the story in his or her own words and explain the Lepcha and Limbu history of the village. Allow about 1.5 hours. Treat it as you would any place of local memory: listen, ask questions, and do not climb on structures under construction. Combine it with the farm walk or a visit to Tharpu.

faqs.q: Is the Stairway to Heaven in Daramdin finished?
faqs.a: Not as far as we know. Wikipedia records that its foundation was laid in 1997 and that work stopped and later resumed. The state of the site changes, so check current status before you travel. The story is the reason to go, and local people tell it whatever the building looks like.

faqs.q: Is the clay-pot tower story a Lepcha legend?
faqs.a: The Soreng district administration presents it as a Lepcha story tied to Daramdin, and quotes the Lepcha words shouted from the top of the tower. We tell it as village tradition, not as a dated event. Ask your guide or homestay host for their version; details vary between families.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at the Stairway to Heaven site?
faqs.a: About an hour to 1.5 hours with a guide, including the walk and time to hear the story. It is a short visit, so pair it with a walk through Daramdin's fields, the Sarva Dharma Kendra, or the Mangardzong site at Tharpu, about 6 km down the road.

experiences.title: An evening with a Limbu or Lepcha host family
experiences.summary: Stay a night with a Limbu or Lepcha family in Daramdin, eat what the household eats and hear how they keep their language, food and festivals alive. Simple rooms, honest prices and conversation are the whole point.
body: Wikipedia describes Daramdin as mostly Limbu and Lepcha, and the 2011 census found Limbu to be the first language of about 14 percent of people in what is now Soreng district, second only to Nepali. In a homestay here you are a guest in a working farmhouse. Rooms are simple, bathrooms may be shared, and meals are what the family cooks that day: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, pickles, perhaps chicken or pork, and tea at any hour.

Ask questions and let your hosts lead. Limbu families may talk about the Mundhum, the body of oral tradition, about Chasok Tangnam, the harvest festival offered to Yuma Sammang, or about the Limbu script. Lepcha hosts may share their own names for the hills and rivers. Not every family wants to talk about history and religion with strangers, so follow their cue, and ask before photographing people, shrines or rituals.

Expect about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with meals, paid in cash. Book through us or ask in the bazaar; the district site lists several homestays. Bring a torch, a warm layer for evenings and slippers. In return for the hospitality, eat what is offered, keep noise down after dark and help clear your plates, as you would in any family home.

faqs.q: Are there Limbu homestays in Daramdin?
faqs.a: Yes. Daramdin's villages are mostly Limbu and Lepcha, and several families take guests. The district administration lists homestays such as Dzoom Lyang, Sai Shruti and Orange Valley. Confirm they are operating and what they include when you book, or ask us to arrange one.

faqs.q: What food is served in a Daramdin homestay?
faqs.a: Home food: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, pickles and often chicken or pork, with tea. Limbu households may serve dishes such as fermented soybean or bamboo shoot. Tell your hosts in advance if you are vegetarian or have allergies; most families are happy to adjust.

faqs.q: Is a homestay in Daramdin suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, for families comfortable with simple rooms and shared spaces. The altitude of about 950 m is low and the farmland around the village is easy walking. Bring a torch, mosquito repellent in the warmer months and anything specific your children need, as shops are small.

experiences.title: Farm walk across Daramdin's flat fields
experiences.summary: Walk the broad fields that gave Daramdin its Lepcha name, past paddy, maize, vegetables, orange trees and, as the district site notes, rose farms. Easy walking by Sikkim standards and best in the harvest months of October and November.
body: Daramdin is one of the few places in Soreng district where you can walk for an hour without climbing hard. The fields spread around the bazaar in wide terraces: paddy that is transplanted in June and July and harvested in October and November, maize in summer, mustard and vegetables in winter, and orange trees around the houses. The district administration also lists rose farming among the activities here, so ask your guide whether any farms are open to visitors.

Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016, and the district site describes how farmers here use cow dung, urine and traditional methods instead of chemical inputs. A local guide can explain the year on these fields: when paddy is planted, how maize and millet are stored, where cardamom is grown on the shadier slopes, and how many households now combine farming with homestays or jobs in town.

Allow two to three hours at an easy pace. Wear shoes with grip, since the field edges are narrow and slippery after rain, carry water and a hat, and stay on bunds and paths rather than walking through crops. October and November bring harvest activity and clear views; from June to September expect mud, leeches and heavy showers.

faqs.q: What crops grow around Daramdin?
faqs.a: Paddy, maize, mustard and vegetables on the flat fields, oranges around houses and cardamom on shadier slopes. The Soreng district site also lists rose farming at Daramdin. What you see depends on the month: harvest in October and November is the busiest and most photogenic time.

faqs.q: Is the Daramdin farm walk easy?
faqs.a: Yes, by Sikkim standards. Daramdin's name means flat land and the fields are gentle, though bunds are narrow and paths can be muddy. Most families and fit seniors manage two to three hours with breaks. Wear shoes with grip and carry water.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the farm walk?
faqs.a: Not to find your way, but a local guide, about ₹500–1,000, makes the walk far more interesting by explaining the crops, introducing you to farmers and keeping you on paths owners are happy for visitors to use. Ask your homestay host to suggest someone.

experiences.title: A quiet stop at the Sarva Dharma Kendra
experiences.summary: Stop at the Sri Sathya Sai Sarva Dharma Kendra in the centre of Daramdin, which Wikipedia names as the village's main attraction. Sarva dharma means all faiths. A calm, short visit on the road between Jorethang and Okhrey.
body: Wikipedia names the Sri Sathya Sai Sarva Dharma Kendra, in the centre of Daramdin, as the village's main attraction. Sarva dharma means all faiths, and the name reflects the teaching of Sathya Sai Baba, the Indian spiritual teacher, that different religions share a common core. It is a place of worship and community activity, not a monument, so expect a quiet compound rather than a tourist site.

Visitors are generally welcome to walk in quietly. Dress modestly, remove shoes where asked, switch phones to silent and follow any timings or rules posted at the entrance. Ask before taking photographs inside. If prayers or bhajans are under way, sit at the back or come back later. There is no entry fee; leave a small donation only if you wish.

Allow about 45 minutes. The Kendra is an easy stop on the drive up to Sombaria and Okhrey or down to Jorethang, and pairs with the Stairway to Heaven site and a walk through the fields. We do not have reliable opening hours, so check locally on the day; mornings are usually the best time.

faqs.q: What is the Sri Sathya Sai Sarva Dharma Kendra in Daramdin?
faqs.a: It is a centre linked to the teachings of Sathya Sai Baba, in the middle of Daramdin, which Wikipedia names as the village's main attraction. Sarva dharma means all faiths. It is a working place of worship and community activity, so visit quietly and follow the rules posted at the gate.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee or dress code at the Kendra?
faqs.a: We are not aware of an entry fee. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, remove shoes where asked and keep phones silent. Rules and timings can change, so check at the entrance on the day and ask before taking photographs inside.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Kendra take?
faqs.a: About 30–45 minutes is enough for most visitors. It makes a calm break on the drive between Jorethang and Okhrey, and combines well with the Stairway to Heaven site and a short walk through Daramdin's fields.

faqs.q: Is Daramdin worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, for travellers who want a farming village with very few tourists, a Lepcha story with a place attached to it and homestays with Limbu or Lepcha families. There are no big sights or viewpoints. One night works well on the way to Okhrey and Barsey, or as a base for Tharpu and Mangardzong.

faqs.q: Where is Daramdin?
faqs.a: In the south-west of Soreng district, about 29 km above Jorethang on the road to Sombaria, Okhrey and Hilley, and about 15 km from Soreng town. The district site places it at about 27.136 N, 88.172 E. Tharpu is about 6 km below and Sombaria about 7 km above.

faqs.q: What does the name Daramdin mean?
faqs.a: The Soreng district administration says it comes from the Lepcha word dalom, meaning a place of rest or a flat land. That suits the village, which has broad, gently sloping fields, rare in this steep part of Sikkim. Wikipedia gives the same explanation.

faqs.q: How do I reach Daramdin from Siliguri?
faqs.a: By shared jeep, go from Siliguri to Jorethang (about 3.5–4 hours, ₹250–350), then take a jeep to Daramdin (1–1.5 hours, ₹80–150). By car it is about 4–5 hours via Sevoke, Melli and Jorethang. NH10 closes after monsoon slides; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Daramdin?
faqs.a: About 950 m, making it one of the lower and warmer villages in Soreng district. Winter days often reach the high teens °C and nights fall to around 6–8 °C. There is no altitude concern at all, which makes it comfortable for older travellers and small children.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Daramdin?
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need a special permit for Daramdin. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India since January 2026. Sikkim's ₹50 tourist fee is collected by your accommodation. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which communities live in Daramdin?
faqs.a: Wikipedia notes that Daramdin is mostly Limbu and Lepcha, with Pradhan, Chettri, Bhujel and other Nepali-speaking families too. Across Soreng district, the 2011 census found Nepali the most common first language, followed by Limbu at about 14 percent. Homestays here are a good way to learn about both communities.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Daramdin?
faqs.a: October to April, when days are dry and mild. November is especially good, with paddy harvest and oranges ripening. Because it is low, Daramdin gets warm and humid from May, and June to September bring heavy rain, leeches and occasional road blocks.

faqs.q: Can I combine Daramdin with Okhrey and Barsey?
faqs.a: Yes, they are on the same road. Daramdin is about 7 km below Sombaria, and Okhrey about 14 km beyond. A typical plan is one night in Daramdin, then two in Okhrey for the Barsey walk from Hilley. This breaks the long drive from Siliguri and adds a village most visitors miss.
